I'm curious what "fork here" in Rserve 1.8-1 really does. 

This is description in the NEWS file:  ... "fork here" directive which allows to spawn multiple pre-forked instances of Rserve which all share the same  memory. ". When looking closer I get the impression that "fork here" defines the line/place where a newly forked instance stops reading and interpreting the config file and so improves fork() time (while forking itself remains the same).

Could you please describe the "fork here" directive?

On Dec 1, 2014, at 11:15 AM, Friedrich Schuster <Friedrich.Schuster at analytical-software.de> wrote:

> 
> Hello, 
> 
> I'm curious what "fork here" in Rserve 1.8-1 really does. 
> 
> This is description in the NEWS file:  ... "fork here" directive which allows to spawn multiple pre-forked instances of Rserve which all share the same  memory. ".  So I can span multiple individual instances and use them individually as some kind of connection pool? But there is no information on how to use the instances. Or how many instances there are. 
> 
> When looking closer I get the impression that "fork here" defines the line/place where a newly forked instance stops reading and interpreting the config file and so improves fork() time (while forking itself remains the same).
> 

Exactly. It was introduced for very specific tasks that use Rserve for very small requests (literally a hash look-up let's say), where the fork() time matters even though it's minimal (~4ms on our severs), because it is serial time. In this rather specific case it is beneficial to start multiple Rserve instances as to leverage multiple cores since each core will be serving connections requests in parallel, thus increasing the request throughput on a multi-core machine. So in the above example the upper bound on requests is 250 requests/s regardless of the number of cores since the server is run on one core until fork() finishes, but if you spawn multiple servers you can increase it to almost 2k/s on an 8-core machine.

The usage is simple, in the above case they would just run each server on a different port and assign clients randomly. The config file for let's say four servers then looks like this:

# ... regular conf directives here ...
port 6300
fork here
port 6301
fork here
port 6302
fork here
port 6303

Cheers,
Simon

Hi all,
I'm starting Rserve in a java thread as follows: 

debug = false;
cmd = "Path_To_R";rargs = "--no-save --slave";rsrvargs = "--no-save --slave --RS-enable-control";
p = Runtime.getRuntime().exec("\""+cmd+"\" -e \"library(Rserve);Rserve("+(debug?"TRUE":"FALSE")+",args='"+rsrvargs+"')\" "+rargs);
Under Linux, I'm able to get spawned a separate instance each time I open en new "RConnection" (through the main instance), but under windows, I get a completely different behaviour: Once the server has been instantiated for the very first time, any new connection I create tries to execute / evaluate on the same single instance. This results in having a single core in use as well as a blocked instance (until the evaluation is done). No way to get several evalutions asynchronously.
I tried some arguments combinations like with/without "--vanilla" or removing "--RS-enable-control", but no effect.As well as starting Rserve directly from R:  
library(Rserve);Rserve(FALSE, args="--no-save --no-restore --slave", wait=T)... (I read somewhere that 'wait' is defaulted to FALSE under Windows and to TRUE everywhere else)...


What did I miss? Why is that working like a charme under Linux and not at all under Windows? Should I expect the right behaviour under MacOSX?
My question could probably be more detailed, but I suspect this is a very common issue I get here.
Any help would be greatly apreciated. Thanks for your time.
RegardsGauthier

Because Windows is not a unix operating system and is much more limited. Unlike modern operating systems Windows lacks support for copy-on-write forking and thus is limited to a single core for interpreted R.

Well, you'll find this on the main Rserve page:

"Although Rserve works on Windows it is not recommended to use it on that platform. Hi,

I have a quite big table in Java (let's say 200 columns and 3.000.000
rows). I can access it rowwise in Java. Column types are different basic
data types (integer, string, ...).
What would be the best/fastest way to transfer it to R via an RServe
connection?
Currently, I am filling one array per column by reading the whole table and
then use these arrays to create an RList. But I'm not sure whether this is
very efficient (concerning memory and speed). And sometimes it even fails
as the connection has a certain transfer limit (as far as I understood).
Any suggestions?

Antje

messages.body_plain:
> On Dec 9, 2014, at 8:45 AM, Antje Janosch <antje.janosch at web.de> wrote:
> 
> Hi,
> 
> I have a quite big table in Java (let's say 200 columns and 3.000.000 rows). I can access it rowwise in Java. Column types are different basic data types (integer, string, ...).
> What would be the best/fastest way to transfer it to R via an RServe connection?
> Currently, I am filling one array per column by reading the whole table and then use these arrays to create an RList. But I'm not sure whether this is very efficient (concerning memory and speed). And sometimes it even fails as the connection has a certain transfer limit (as far as I understood).
> Any suggestions?
> 

It is almost the most efficient way. Depending on your R version, the most memory-efficient way may be to push them one column at a time since that reduces the memory used for transfer at the cost of multiple roundtrips. The alternative for R versions that don't have shallow copy is to assign each column to a variable and then construct the data frame from them. You certainly want to remove the upload limit in the config file - it's a safety measure that you can disable if your machine has enough memory.

Note that in either case you want to create the data.frame "by hand" (attach row.names and class attributes to a list) not by calling data.frame()/as.data.frame() since those are very slow for big data frames.

Cheers,
Simon

> Can you provide me a link concerning your comment on the 'shallow copy' thing? I was not aware that there were changes with newer R-versions and I don't know how these changes look like.

---
NEWS R 3.1.0:

• Avoid duplicating the right hand side values in complex assignments when possible. This reduces copying of replacement values in expressions such as Z$a <- a0 and ans[[i]] <- tmp: some package code has relied on there being copies.

Also, a number of other changes to reduce copying of objects; all contributed by or based on suggestions by Michael Lawrence.
---

What this means is that 

l=list()
l[[1]]=...
l[[2]]=...

is efficient since it doesn't copy the previous columns on each assignment (which older R versions did).

If you want to avoid all copying, you'd use vector("list", n) to pre-allocate the columns, obviously.


> It's also a good comment to switch off the upload limit. I though it would use some default then.
> 

The config setting is maxinbuf and you set it to kB of size, so let's say if you want to process at most 1Gb packets, you'd use

maxinbuf 1048576

The default is 256Mb. In most cases the limit should not exceed half of the available memory.

Cheers,
Simon

Yes, using control commands (serverEval/serverSource). The existing client sessions don't need to be stopped since they are independent of the server. However, the server will queue up new connection requests until the evaluation finishes.

messages.body_plain:
I believe I've found the answer to my question. I now see that their are
two methods:

.jserialize
.junserialize

That call custom methods implemented on the RJavaClassLoader. These methods
offer the same functionality as writing to and reading from
Object[Output|Input]Stream objects and work with classes available on the
RJavaClassLoader. In my code above, serializeObject(object, filename) can
be replace with

serializeObject <- function(object, filename) {
  file.con <- file(filename, "wb")
  writeBin(.jserialize(object), file.con)
  flush(file.con)
  close(file.con)
}

and deserializeObject(filename) can be replace with:

deserializeObject <- function(filename) {
  file.con <- file(filename, "rb")
  file.size <- file.info(filename)$size
  data <- readBin(file.con, raw(), file.size)
  close(file.con)
  object <- .junserialize(file.con)
}

I've verified that the files created are identical to the ones that would
be created with ObjectOutputStream, so they can be used to reconstruct any
saved objects outside of R (i.e. if using Weka or some other library
directly from java).

Thanks!
